title: The Old Tree Behind My Childhood House
script: Narrator: [warmly] Behind my childhood house stood a huge old banyan tree that my grandfather said was already tall before he was even born.
Narrator: As kids, my cousins and I climbed its thick branches every afternoon, although our mothers constantly told us to be more careful.
Narrator: [concerned] I never really thought about the tree as something fragile, because it had always been there, exactly the same, throughout my whole childhood.
Narrator: Last year, a strong storm hit our village, and when I finally visited home again, half the tree had fallen during the heavy wind.
Narrator: [honestly] I stood there looking at the broken branches for a long time, feeling a sadness I didn't fully expect to feel.
Narrator: My father noticed me standing there and said, it's just a tree, son, although I could tell even he felt something similar.
Narrator: [relieved] I realized I wasn't only sad about the tree itself, but about how quickly things I assumed were permanent could actually change.
Narrator: That night, I asked my grandfather if he was sad too, since he had known that tree even longer than my father had.
Narrator: [thoughtful] He said something I still think about often. He said, nothing in nature is truly permanent, so we should appreciate it while it stands.
Narrator: The remaining half of the tree is still alive, though smaller now, and new branches have already started growing from where it broke.
Narrator: [reflective] My father planted a young banyan sapling nearby too, so that eventually, when the old tree finally dies, something will already be growing to replace it.
Narrator: I visited again last month and sat under what remains of that ancient tree, listening to the same birds that used to wake me as a child.
Narrator: [peacefully] I think about my grandfather's words whenever I pass any old tree now, because they taught me something simple but important about paying attention while things last.

quiz.question: What kind of tree stood behind the narrator's childhood house?
options: A small palm tree
A huge old banyan tree
A young mango tree
A pine tree
quiz.explanation: A huge old banyan tree stood behind the house, already tall before his grandfather was born.

quiz.question: What happened to the tree during a storm last year?
options: Nothing happened
Half of it fell during heavy wind
It was cut down deliberately
It grew taller
quiz.explanation: A strong storm hit the village, and half the tree had fallen during the heavy wind.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's grandfather say about the tree?
options: Trees should always be cut down eventually
The tree was never important
He never noticed the tree at all
Nothing in nature is truly permanent, so we should appreciate it while it stands
quiz.explanation: His grandfather said nothing in nature is truly permanent, so people should appreciate it while it stands.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's father do after the storm?
options: He removed the remaining tree completely
He planted a young banyan sapling nearby
He built a fence around it
He ignored the damage
quiz.explanation: The father planted a young banyan sapling nearby so something would already be growing when the old tree eventually dies.

quiz.question: What is the narrator's final lesson from this experience?
options: To pay attention to things while they last
To avoid old trees
To never visit his childhood home again
That storms are always destructive with no benefit
quiz.explanation: He concludes his grandfather's words taught him something important about paying attention while things last.

quiz.question: Why did the damage feel surprising?
options: The storm had been very small
The family planned to cut it down
The grandfather had planted it recently
The tree had seemed permanent throughout the narrator’s life
quiz.explanation: Long familiarity created an assumption of permanence.

quiz.question: What does the father’s reaction suggest?
options: His words minimized the loss, but he also felt attached
He disliked the tree
He caused the storm damage
He wanted to remove the remaining half
quiz.explanation: The narrator notices emotion beneath “just a tree.”

quiz.question: How does new growth complicate the loss?
options: The old tree becomes unchanged
The sapling immediately replaces the shade
Damage and continued life exist at the same time
Storms always improve trees
quiz.explanation: The scene contains both grief and recovery.

quiz.question: Why plant a sapling before the old tree dies?
options: The remaining tree is already dead
Young trees prevent all storm damage
Future shade and continuity require time to develop
The grandfather requested identical branches
quiz.explanation: Replacement planning begins before mature benefits disappear.

quiz.question: What does listening to the same birds connect?
options: The sapling with city traffic
Present change with childhood memory
The storm with the mother’s warning
The father with another village
quiz.explanation: Sound gives continuity even though the tree has changed.
